passage: The school bus had already left the kasba square when Kiran hovered by the staffroom door, dupatta twisted around one finger. Salma ma'am was marking copies. "Ma'am... can I ask something? You won't laugh?" "Sit." Kiran sat on the edge of the chair. "Everyone says I should be a doctor because I got good marks. But I feel dizzy when I see blood. Is that stupid?" She watched Salma ma'am's mouth for a smile. None came. "It's a real question. What part of medicine pulls you, and what part scares you?" Kiran's shoulders dropped an inch. "The part where you work out what's wrong," she said, and pulled the chair closer.

qa.q: What was Kiran twisting around one finger?
qa.a: Kiran had her dupatta twisted around one finger.

qa.q: Why did Kiran watch Salma ma'am's mouth for a smile?
qa.a: She was afraid her doubt would be laughed at 😰, so she was testing whether the teacher would take her seriously.

qa.q: What turning point does Salma ma'am offer at this stage, and how?
qa.a: By calling it a real question and asking what pulls and scares her, she treats Kiran's doubt with respect, which invites her to open up further.

qa.q: What might Salma ma'am be noticing as Kiran pulls the chair closer?
qa.a: Likely that Kiran's guard is dropping and trust is beginning, and that this student has thought carefully about her future.

grounding: A teenage girl brings her doubts about becoming a doctor to a teacher, tests for mockery, and relaxes when met with respect.

passage: Rain streaked the windows of the biology lab in Toronto. Rania lingered after the others left, pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean. Ms Jin looked up from her laptop. "Something on your mind?" "Kind of." Rania laughed, too quickly. "My parents think I'm going to med school. I'm not sure I even want to. Probably sounds dumb." "It doesn't." Ms Jin closed the laptop. "Tell me what you're not sure about." Rania talked for a minute, then stopped, checking her face. Ms Jin only nodded and waited. So Rania kept going, and this time she sat down.

qa.q: What was Rania pretending to do after class?
qa.a: She was pretending to wipe a bench that was already clean.

qa.q: What does Rania's quick laugh and "Probably sounds dumb" suggest?
qa.a: She is nervous about being judged and protects herself by mocking her own doubt before anyone else can.

qa.q: Which small move by Ms Jin lowered Rania's guard?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and asking what she wasn't sure about showed full attention and respect, so Rania felt safe to keep talking and sit down.

qa.q: If Ms Jin had joked about it, what would change for Rania?
qa.a: She would probably have left quickly and kept her doubts private, missing the chance to think them through with an adult she trusts.

grounding: A teenage girl tests whether her teacher will take her doubts about medicine seriously, and each respectful reply lowers her guard.

passage:
The Ahmedabad school corridor was empty by four o'clock. Hansa stood outside the staffroom for a full minute before going in. Wasim sir was sorting lab reports.
"Sir, can I ask something... not about the syllabus?"
"Sit."
She didn't. "Everyone at home says I'll be a doctor. But I faint at blood tests." She watched his face for the laugh.
It didn't come. He put the reports down. "That's worth thinking about properly. What do you like about medicine?"
She sat then. "Figuring out why people are ill."
"Then there's more than one road." Her grip on her bag strap loosened a little.

qa.q: How long did Hansa stand outside the staffroom?
qa.a: A full minute.

qa.q: Why did Hansa watch Wasim sir's face after telling him about fainting?
qa.a: She was nervous and guarded, testing whether he would laugh at her doubt or take it seriously.

qa.q: What turning point does this conversation offer Hansa?
qa.a: She now has an adult who takes her doubts seriously, so she could keep exploring what she enjoys about medicine.

qa.q: What might Wasim sir be experiencing as she finally sits down?
qa.a: He may feel quietly pleased and careful, sensing her trust is new and easily broken.

grounding: Shows a student testing a teacher with her doubts about becoming a doctor, and his respectful replies lowering her guard.

passage:
"Ma'am, are you busy?"
"Not for you, Payal. Come."
Payal hovered by Reena ma'am's desk. "This is maybe silly."
"Try me."
"My parents want me to do medicine. I'm good at biology. But I don't know if I want it or they want it."
She stopped, bracing.
"That's not silly. That's a grown-up question," Reena ma'am said. "When you imagine being a doctor, what do you feel?"
"Tired. And proud. Both."
"Both is honest. Shall we look at what doctors actually do in a day, next week?"
Payal pulled a chair closer. "Can I bring my list of questions?"

qa.q: What did Payal say she feels when she imagines being a doctor?
qa.a: Tired. And proud. Both.

qa.q: What does Payal's hovering suggest she felt at first?
qa.a: She hovered, called her question maybe silly and stopped bracing, which shows she was anxious about being laughed at.

qa.q: Which reply from Reena ma'am helped most, and why?
qa.a: Calling it a grown-up question, because it showed Payal her doubt was taken seriously.

qa.q: What might Reena ma'am feel when Payal pulls a chair closer?
qa.a: She is probably pleased and touched that Payal is starting to trust her enough to come back.

grounding: Shows a student testing whether her teacher will take her doubts about medicine seriously and relaxing as each reply is respectful.

passage:
I still remember the first time I went to Tanuja ma'am's desk after school. I was the girl who never spoke in chemistry, and my ears were hot. I said I wasn't sure I wanted to be a doctor, even though my whole family had decided I would. I waited for her to laugh, or to say "Arre, everyone is scared at first."
She didn't. She asked what part scared me. I said the years. The pressure. She wrote it down, like it mattered. Then she asked what part I liked, and wrote that down too.
I went back the next week. And the next. Each time, I said a little more. That's how I, Gopika, started trusting a teacher.

qa.q: What did Tanuja ma'am do after asking what part scared Gopika?
qa.a: She wrote it down, like it mattered.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling while waiting at the desk?
qa.a: Gopika was nervous and embarrassed, ears hot, expecting to be laughed at or brushed off.

qa.q: What is the turning point Tanuja ma'am offers at this stage?
qa.a: Writing down both the fears and the likes, which treats Gopika's doubt as real and invites her back.

qa.q: How might Tanuja ma'am see Gopika's visits each week?
qa.a: She may notice Gopika saying a little more each time and feel hopeful that trust is growing.

grounding: Shows a student testing a teacher with doubts about becoming a doctor and slowly lowering her guard as each reply is respectful.

passage: Teacher's notebook, Afreen Ma'am, Biology, Thursday. Hafsa came to my desk after school again, the third time this month. She hovers first, pretending to read the notice board. Today she finally said, "Ma'am, can I ask something stupid?" I said there was no such thing. She asked whether it was wrong to want to be a doctor if she feels faint at the sight of blood. She watched my face closely, as if waiting for me to laugh. I didn't. I told her it was a real question, and that some doctors work in labs or research and rarely see blood. Her shoulders came down. Then she told me more: her family expects medicine, and she isn't sure she wants it at all. We will meet again next week, and I'll bring information on other paths too.

qa.q: What did Hafsa ask before her real question?
qa.a: She asked, "Ma'am, can I ask something stupid?"

qa.q: Why did Hafsa watch Afreen Ma'am's face so closely?
qa.a: She was nervous and unsure, testing whether the teacher would take her seriously or laugh at her worry about blood.

qa.q: What made Hafsa open up further?
qa.a: Afreen Ma'am treated the question as real and answered respectfully, which lowered Hafsa's guard enough to share her family's expectations.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's family see her doubts?
qa.a: Her family expects medicine, so they may be surprised or worried to learn she isn't sure she wants it.

grounding: Shows a student cautiously bringing doubts about becoming a doctor to a teacher, testing the reaction, and relaxing with each respectful reply.
